title: Postnatal red flags and escalation
blurb: Recognise the NICE NG194 warning symptoms after birth, link each to its likely cause, and escalate postnatal hypertension and suspected sepsis correctly.
question: On day 4 at home, Hana, 33, who had pre-eclampsia, tells the community midwife she has a headache that will not go away and her vision is blurry. Her BP is 156/102. What does this suggest and what should the midwife do?

teach.h: Red flags: symptoms that cannot wait
teach.body: Formally: NICE NG194 1.2.4 lists symptoms and signs of potentially serious conditions that a woman should seek medical advice for without delay. In plain English: most postnatal aches and changes are normal, but a short list of symptoms can signal haemorrhage, infection, a clot, pre-eclampsia or mastitis. The midwife teaches this list at the first postnatal contact and acts at once when she sees any item on it.

teach.h: NG194 1.2.4: symptom and what it could mean
head: Symptom or sign
Could indicate
rows: Sudden, very heavy, persistent or increasing bleeding
Abdominal, pelvic or perineal pain, fever, shivering, smelly discharge
Leg swelling and tenderness, or shortness of breath
Hypertension, pre-eclampsia, post-dural puncture headache, migraine, infection
Breast redness and swelling over 24 h despite self-care
teach.caption: Also: any symptoms or signs of a potentially serious condition that do not respond to treatment.

steps.label: Escalate
steps.sub: Refer without delay; 999 if critically ill

teach.caption: All healthcare professionals should ensure appropriate referral if there are concerns about the woman's health (NG194 1.2.6).

teach.h: Sepsis: within 6 weeks she is high risk
teach.body: NICE NG255 places anyone pregnant or within 6 weeks of birth, termination or miscarriage in a high-risk group for sepsis, especially after caesarean, operative birth, removal of retained products, prolonged rupture of membranes, or with continued bleeding or offensive discharge. Sepsis can be afebrile. Outside hospital, any high-risk criterion (for example RR 25 or more, HR over 130, systolic 90 or less, new confusion, mottled skin) means emergency transfer, usually by 999, with a pre-alert. If puerperal sepsis is suspected, assess the baby for infection too.

teach.caption: On treatment: consider reducing it if BP falls below 140/90 and reduce it below 130/80 (NG133 1.5.17). Transfer to community when there are no symptoms, BP is 150/100 or less and bloods are stable or improving (1.5.19).

items: Not on treatment: measure BP at least 4 times a day while an inpatient, at least once on days 3 to 5, then on alternate days until normal if abnormal on days 3 to 5.
Start antihypertensive treatment if BP is 150/100 mmHg or higher.
Ask about severe headache and epigastric pain each time BP is measured (1.5.15).
Stop methyldopa within 2 days of the birth; enalapril is the first choice postnatally, including with breastfeeding.
Medical review 2 weeks after transfer if still on treatment, and for all at 6 to 8 weeks after the birth.

teach.h: Breast symptoms: self-care or seek advice?

children.label: Keep feeding, check attachment, rest, analgesia

teach.body: Hana had pre-eclampsia and now has a persistent headache, blurred vision and BP 156/102. NG194 lists persistent or severe headache as a red flag for pre-eclampsia and hypertension, and her BP is above the 150/100 treatment threshold. The midwife does not reassure and wait: she arranges same-day medical review in line with local pathways, checks for epigastric pain and other symptoms, and documents clearly.

teach.text: Pre-eclampsia does not end at birth. A postnatal headache in a woman who had pre-eclampsia is not "just tiredness". Also remember: postnatal antihypertensive treatment starts at 150/100, not the antenatal 140/90.

items: Teach the NG194 1.2.4 red flags at the first postnatal midwife contact.
Heavy or increasing bleeding: retained tissue or endometritis. Pain, fever, smell: infection.
Leg swelling, breathlessness or chest pain: VTE. Severe headache: pre-eclampsia among others.
Up to 6 weeks after birth she is in the sepsis high-risk group; sepsis can be afebrile.
Postnatal: start antihypertensives at 150/100 or more; enalapril first choice.

summary: You can now teach and recognise the NICE postnatal red flags, link each to its likely cause, and escalate without delay. You can also apply the postnatal BP thresholds after pre-eclampsia and the sepsis high-risk rules for the first 6 weeks.

A.q: Joy, 29, is 8 days postnatal. She has a swollen, tender left calf. Which condition should the midwife suspect first?
options: Venous thromboembolism
Postnatal pre-eclampsia
Endometritis
Pelvic girdle pain
A.why: NG194 1.2.4: leg swelling and tenderness, or shortness of breath, could indicate venous thromboembolism.

whyNot.1: Pre-eclampsia is suggested by headache, visual disturbance or raised BP, not unilateral calf swelling.
whyNot.2: Endometritis presents with abnormal bleeding, pelvic pain, fever or offensive discharge.
whyNot.3: Pelvic girdle pain affects the pelvis and does not cause a swollen, tender calf.

A.q: At the first postnatal visit, the midwife explains breast symptoms that need medical advice. Which description is correct?
options: Fullness in both breasts around day 3 after the birth
Nipple tenderness at the start of each feed
Leaking milk between feeds in the first weeks
Redness and swelling over 24 h despite self-care
A.why: NG194 1.2.4: worsening reddening and swelling of the breasts persisting for more than 24 hours despite self-management could indicate mastitis.

whyNot.0: Fullness around days 2 to 4 is the milk coming in and is expected.
whyNot.1: Early tenderness should prompt a check of attachment, but it is not the NG194 red flag.
whyNot.2: Leaking between feeds is common and is not a warning sign.

A.q: Up to how long after giving birth does NICE NG255 place a woman in the high-risk group for sepsis?
options: 2 weeks
6 weeks
12 weeks
6 months
A.why: NG255 1.2.1: people who are pregnant or have been pregnant in the past 6 weeks (birth, termination or miscarriage) are in the high-risk group.

whyNot.0: 2 weeks is too short; the NG255 window is 6 weeks.
whyNot.2: 12 weeks is twice the NG255 window; the high-risk group covers the 6 weeks after birth (1.2.1).
whyNot.3: 6 months is longer than the NG255 definition.

B.q: Bea, 31, had pre-eclampsia and is not on antihypertensives. On day 2 on the postnatal ward her BP is 152/101. What does NICE NG133 recommend?
options: Recheck at the GP 6 to 8 week review
Start antihypertensive treatment
Restart methyldopa from pregnancy
Recheck once on day 5 at home
B.why: NG133 1.5.14: in women with pre-eclampsia who did not take antihypertensive treatment, start treatment after the birth if BP is 150/100 mmHg or higher.

whyNot.0: Leaving a BP above the treatment threshold until 6 to 8 weeks is unsafe.
whyNot.2: Methyldopa should be stopped within 2 days of the birth; enalapril is the first choice postnatally.
whyNot.3: Inpatients with pre-eclampsia need BP checked at least 4 times a day, and this reading already needs treatment.

B.q: Tia, 26, is 5 days after an emergency caesarean. On a home visit she is confused, her RR is 26 and her HR is 134. Her temperature is 36.8 C. What should the midwife do?
options: Call 999 for emergency transfer with a pre-alert
Arrange a GP appointment for later this afternoon
Repeat full observations in 1 hour and reassess
Advise paracetamol, oral fluids and rest at home
B.why: NG255: new altered mental state, RR 25 or more and HR over 130 are high-risk criteria. Outside hospital, any high-risk criterion means emergency transfer, usually by 999, with a pre-alert (1.6.1-1.6.2). A normal temperature does not exclude sepsis.

whyNot.1: A GP appointment later in the day delays treatment of possible high-risk sepsis.
whyNot.2: Repeating observations in an hour delays the emergency response NG255 requires.
whyNot.3: Self-care advice would be unsafe with high-risk sepsis criteria.

B.q: Rachel, 34, is 10 days postnatal and suddenly breathless with chest pain. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Advise rest and review at the next visit
Treat as possible anxiety and refer to the GP
Arrange emergency assessment for possible VTE
Advise her to stop breastfeeding to rest
B.why: NG194 1.2.4: shortness of breath and chest pain could indicate VTE or cardiac problems. Thrombosis and thromboembolism is the leading cause of maternal death during pregnancy and up to 6 weeks after (MBRRACE-UK 2022-24), so she needs emergency assessment.

whyNot.0: Waiting for the next visit could be fatal if she has a pulmonary embolism.
whyNot.1: Labelling this as anxiety risks missing a life-threatening clot.
whyNot.3: Stopping breastfeeding does nothing for possible VTE and removes protection for the baby.

C.q: Ellie, 27, is day 6 after a vaginal birth with retained products removed. She reports offensive lochia, lower abdominal pain and shivers. Her baby is breastfeeding. Besides arranging urgent assessment for Ellie, what else should the midwife do?
options: Advise her to stop breastfeeding until treated
Assess the baby for signs of infection
Start oral antibiotics from her home supply
Arrange a review of the baby at 6 weeks
C.why: NG194 1.2.8: if the woman has confirmed or suspected puerperal sepsis, assess the baby for symptoms or signs of infection.

whyNot.0: Puerperal sepsis is not a reason to stop breastfeeding; the NG194 action is to assess the baby.
whyNot.2: Midwives do not start antibiotics from a home supply; she needs medical assessment and prescribing.
whyNot.3: Waiting 6 weeks ignores the baby's current infection risk.

C.q: Noor, 30, had an epidural and is 2 days postnatal. She has a severe headache that is worse when she sits up and eases when lying flat. Her BP is 118/76. Which statement is most accurate?
options: Postural headache with normal BP is expected and needs no review
This rules out all serious causes because the BP is normal
Advise her to stay upright to help the headache settle
Possible post-dural puncture headache needing medical review
C.why: NG194 1.2.4 lists persistent or severe headache as a red flag, with causes including post-dural puncture headache, hypertension, pre-eclampsia, migraine, intracranial pathology and infection. A postural headache after an epidural suggests post-dural puncture headache, which needs anaesthetic review.

whyNot.0: A severe headache is an NG194 red flag and needs review even with normal BP.
whyNot.1: Normal BP lowers the likelihood of pre-eclampsia, but other serious causes remain possible.
whyNot.2: Staying upright worsens a postural headache and does not treat the cause.

C.q: Kemi, 36, had pre-eclampsia and takes enalapril. On day 5 her BP is 148/96, she has no symptoms and her bloods are stable. Is she suitable for transfer to community care?
options: No: she must stay until BP is under 120/80
Yes: she meets the NG133 transfer criteria
No: enalapril must be stopped before transfer
No: she needs a 24-hour urine collection first
C.why: NG133 1.5.19: offer transfer to community care when there are no symptoms of pre-eclampsia, BP is 150/100 mmHg or less (with or without treatment) and blood tests are stable or improving. 148/96 meets this.

whyNot.0: Under 120/80 is not the NG133 transfer criterion.
whyNot.2: Enalapril is the first-choice postnatal antihypertensive and is compatible with breastfeeding.
whyNot.3: Routine 24-hour urine collection is not required; it is not a transfer criterion.

reteach.title: Five systems, five dangers
reteach.question: Group the postnatal red flags by body system and the cause behind each becomes obvious. What are the five groups?

blocks.body: Bleed: heavy or increasing loss (retained tissue, endometritis). Bug: pain, fever, shivers, smelly discharge (infection, possibly sepsis). Clot: leg swelling, breathlessness, chest pain (VTE). Pressure: persistent or severe headache (pre-eclampsia, hypertension, post-dural puncture headache). Breast: redness and swelling over 24 hours despite self-care (mastitis).

blocks.text: A normal temperature does not rule out sepsis. NG255 says sepsis may be non-specific and the woman may be afebrile: look at RR, HR, BP, mental state and skin.

explain.body: Sudden, very heavy, persistent or increasing bleeding may indicate retained placental tissue or endometritis. Abdominal, pelvic or perineal pain, fever, shivering or smelly discharge may indicate infection.

test.q: Day 9 postnatal, Abi's bleeding has suddenly become heavier with clots. What could this indicate?
options: Normal lochia changing colour
Retained placental tissue
The return of her periods
Post-dural puncture leak
test.why: NG194 1.2.4: sudden or very heavy, persistent or increased bleeding could indicate retained placental tissue or endometritis.

whyNot.0: Normal lochia lessens over time; it does not suddenly become heavier with clots.
whyNot.2: Menstruation is not the explanation NICE asks midwives to consider for increasing bleeding at day 9.
whyNot.3: A dural leak causes a postural headache, not vaginal bleeding.

explain.body: Leg swelling and tenderness, or shortness of breath, could indicate VTE. Chest pain could indicate VTE or a cardiac problem. Thrombosis and thromboembolism is the leading cause of maternal death during pregnancy and up to 6 weeks after (MBRRACE-UK 2022-24).

items.label: thrombosis: leading cause of maternal death to 6 weeks

test.q: Which symptom could indicate a cardiac problem as well as VTE after birth?
options: Chest pain
Calf cramp at night
Ankle swelling on both sides
Pelvic girdle pain
test.why: NG194 1.2.4: chest pain could indicate venous thromboembolism or cardiac problems.

whyNot.1: Night cramps are common and are not on the NG194 list.
whyNot.2: Mild symmetrical ankle swelling is common after birth; unilateral swelling with tenderness suggests VTE.
whyNot.3: Pelvic girdle pain is musculoskeletal, not cardiac.

explain.body: Persistent or severe headache could indicate hypertension, pre-eclampsia, post-dural puncture headache, migraine, intracranial pathology or infection. After pre-eclampsia, start antihypertensives at 150/100 or more; enalapril is first choice.

test.q: Which antihypertensive is the first choice after the birth for a woman who is breastfeeding?
options: Methyldopa
Losartan
Enalapril
Furosemide
test.why: NG133 1.9.4: offer enalapril to treat hypertension in the postnatal period, including for women who are breastfeeding (with renal function and potassium monitoring).

whyNot.0: NG133 1.5.18: methyldopa should be stopped within 2 days of the birth and changed to an alternative if needed.
whyNot.1: ARBs such as losartan should be avoided where possible when breastfeeding (NG133 1.9.8).
whyNot.3: Diuretics should be avoided where possible when breastfeeding (NG133 1.9.8).

explain.body: Any NG255 high-risk criterion outside hospital means emergency transfer, usually 999, with a pre-alert. High-risk criteria include new altered mental state, RR 25 or more, HR over 130, systolic 90 or less, no urine for 18 hours, mottled or ashen skin, cyanosis, non-blanching rash.

test.q: At a home visit, Zoe, 24, day 3, has HR 112, RR 22 and temperature 37.9 C, with no other criteria. Which NG255 category does this fit?
options: High risk: call 999 for emergency transfer
Low risk: routine postnatal advice
No sepsis criteria present at this visit
Moderate to high risk: urgent review
test.why: NG255 table 1: HR 100-130 and RR 21-24 are moderate to high risk criteria; outside hospital she needs assessment to reach a diagnosis and decide whether she can be treated safely at home (1.6.5). No high-risk criterion is present.

whyNot.0: None of her values meet a high-risk threshold (HR over 130, RR 25 or more).
whyNot.1: Two moderate to high risk criteria are present, so routine advice is not enough.
whyNot.2: Her HR and RR both fall within moderate to high risk bands.
